text: A board of X's and O's. A region of connected O's is captured — flipped to X — if none of its cells are on the board's edge. Capture all surrounded regions in place.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a whole O region survives if even one of its cells touches an edge; otherwise the entire region flips. Connectivity is four-directional. Is that right?
Exactly — one edge cell saves the whole region.

Then I'll flip the question. Instead of hunting for surrounded regions, I find the safe ones. A region is safe exactly when it's connected to the border. So I DFS from every O on the four edges, marking that whole region with a temporary hash. After that, any O still left was never reached from an edge — it's surrounded — so I flip it to X, and turn the hashes back to O.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to DFS each interior region, collect all its cells, and check if any sits on an edge — but not-surrounded is a property of the whole region, so it's fiddly and easy to get wrong. This problem reminds me of a reverse flood fill from the border: flood from the edges, mark what's reachable, then handle the rest. One linear pass.

Here's the plan. One: for every O on the four borders, run a DFS that marks its region with a hash. Two: the DFS marks the cell, then recurses only into neighbors that are still O. Three: sweep the board — hash goes back to O, everything else becomes X. Here, I'm using the hash as a third symbol for confirmed safe, so the final sweep can tell a safe O apart from a surrounded one. One thing worth flagging — that still-O guard skips walls, already-marked safe cells, and out-of-bounds, so it's my visited check and my obstacle check in one. There's a trade-off here. Mutating the board avoids a separate visited grid, and for a huge all-O board BFS avoids deep recursion, but I'll write DFS. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Two loops walk the left and right edges, then the top and bottom, launching the DFS on any O. The DFS marks its cell with a hash on entry, then only continues into in-bounds neighbors that are still O. A final double loop flips: hash back to O, anything else to X. One thing worth flagging — the board is char, so the quotes matter: O, X and hash are all single-quoted characters, and it's the capital letter O, not the digit zero. Compare against the digit and nothing is ever marked safe, so every O gets captured.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. The four-by-four board: an inner region of three O's, plus one O on the bottom edge. Expected: the inner three flip, the edge one stays. The row that matters is the border scan. The only border O is at row three, column one, and its DFS marks just itself, since it has no O neighbors. The inner region is never reached from any edge, so the sweep flips those three to X, and the edge cell comes back as O. That matches. Let's also test with corner cases. A single X cell stays X. A board where every O touches an edge — like a ring around the border — keeps all of them, since the border floods the whole region.

The time complexity is m times n — the border DFS visits each cell at most once, plus one flip sweep. The space complexity is m times n for the recursion stack in the worst case, a board that's one big connected region of O's. Oh, one more thing — this border-reverse trick is a general tool: when the target is hard to test per cell, flood from the edges and mark, then read off the answer. Here, reached from an edge means safe; the leftover O's are the surrounded ones.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You reversed it — marking safe regions from the border instead of detecting surrounded ones. You used the hash as a third state so the final sweep can separate safe from captured. And you noticed the single not-O guard doubles as visited and obstacle check, tying it back to the border-flood family. Good work.
